title: Key-Value Store With History
statement:
Build a key–value store that remembers every value a key has had, so you can ask what a key held at any moment in the past.

  • TimeMap() creates an empty store.
  • set(key, value, timestamp) records that key holds value from timestamp on. Earlier values are kept.
  • get(key, timestamp) returns the value of the latest set for key whose timestamp is at or before timestamp. If there is none (the key was never set, or only set later), return the empty string "".

Timestamps passed to set are strictly increasing across all calls. Timestamps passed to get can be anything.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the store. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: At time 5 the latest change was at 3, so "light". At exactly 8 the new value already counts. Any later time also sees "dark".
At time 9 "lang" had not been set yet, so there is no value, even though the key exists. "font" was never set at all.

constraints: 1 ≤ key.length, value.length ≤ 50, lowercase letters and digits
Timestamps of set calls are strictly increasing
hints: Group the history by key first. What does one key's history look like, given how set timestamps arrive?
Each key's list of (timestamp, value) pairs is already sorted by timestamp, because set timestamps only grow. You never need to sort.
For get, binary search that list for the last timestamp ≤ the asked time. Find the first timestamp that is greater, then step back one. If you step back past the start, return "".

explain.intuition:
A map from key to its history handles "which key". The interesting part is "which moment". Because set timestamps only grow, appending to a key's list keeps it sorted for free. So get is a binary search: find the last entry whose timestamp is ≤ t. This is how undo stacks, git blame or a "state at commit X" view work: the history is sorted by time, and a lookup asks what was true at a point.

The cleanest way to find "last ≤ t" is to find "first > t" and step back one. "First > t" is a standard search over the half-open range [0, len): it never misses an answer, and its result can be len (everything ≤ t) or 0 (nothing ≤ t, so the answer is "").
steps: Keep a map from key to two parallel arrays: times and values.
set: append to that key's arrays. They stay sorted by time.
get: if the key is missing, return "". Otherwise search [lo, hi) = [0, len): while lo < hi, if times[mid] <= t then lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. Now lo is the first index with a time greater than t.
If lo === 0, nothing was set at or before t: return "". Otherwise return values[lo − 1].
pitfalls: Using times[mid] < t in the search. That finds the first time ≥ t, so a get at exactly a set's timestamp returns the value before it.
Forgetting the case where every stored time is after t. Stepping back from index 0 reads values[-1]: undefined in JavaScript, and the last value in Python, which is silently wrong.
Scanning the history backwards from the end. It is fine when lookups are recent, but asking about the distant past costs O(length of history) every time.

complexity.time: O(1) per set, O(log h) per get, where h is that key's history length

solutions.title: Scan the history backwards
solutions.idea: Store each key's history in order and, on get, walk from the newest entry back until the time is at or before t.

solutions.title: Sorted history per key + binary search
solutions.idea: Append to per-key arrays, which stay sorted because set times grow. On get, find the first time greater than t and step back one.

followups: set calls may now arrive out of order. Which structure keeps each key's history sorted with fast inserts?
Add delete(key, timestamp), after which get returns "" until the key is set again. How do you record that in the history?
